lesson.title: Counting Successes: Building the Binomial Distribution from Scratch
lesson.summary: Once a situation satisfies the binomial conditions, the count of successes becomes a random variable with its own probability distribution spanning every whole number from 0 to n.
lesson.body:
When a situation satisfies the four BINS conditions, the number of successes across all n trials becomes a random variable worth naming. Call it X, the count of successes, and write X ~ B(n, p) to mean X follows a binomial distribution with n trials and success probability p. Unlike a continuous measurement, X can only take whole number values from 0 up through n. There is no such thing as 2.5 successes.

Like any discrete probability distribution, the binomial distribution has to assign a probability to every possible value of X, and those probabilities have to add up to exactly 1. The binomial distribution is really just a specific rule for computing P(X = k) for each k from 0 to n, but before reaching for a formula it helps to build one distribution completely by hand so you can see where those probabilities actually come from.

Flip a fair coin 3 times and let X count the number of heads. Since each flip is independent with the same probability of heads, this is a binomial setting with n = 3 and p = 0.5. There are 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 equally likely outcomes for the sequence of flips: TTT, TTH, THT, HTT, THH, HTH, HHT, and HHH.

Sorting those 8 outcomes by how many heads they contain gives the full distribution. Zero heads happens in only 1 way (TTT), so P(X = 0) = 1/8. One head happens in 3 ways (TTH, THT, HTT), so P(X = 1) = 3/8. Two heads also happens in 3 ways (THH, HTH, HHT), so P(X = 2) = 3/8. Three heads happens in only 1 way (HHH), so P(X = 3) = 1/8. Adding those up, 1/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 + 1/8 = 8/8 = 1, confirming this is a legitimate probability distribution.

Notice the pattern in how many outcomes landed in each category: 1, 3, 3, 1. Those counts are not a coincidence, they come from counting how many different orderings of heads and tails produce a given number of heads. Listing every outcome by hand works fine for 3 flips, but it becomes unmanageable fast (a mere 10 flips already has 1,024 possible sequences). The next chapters build a systematic way to get those counts, and the resulting probabilities, without writing out every outcome.
